EpitomeJob — LLD Bible v2

The development bible. Self-contained: every diagram is inside this one file. Open it anywhere, no other files needed.

Version 2.0, 2026-11-08 | CTO / Chief Solution Architect | Design only — no full code files. Class names, API JSON, table columns and sequences are specified so a developer can write the code without guessing.

What changed from v1 (reviewed 2026-11-08): v1 listed diagram filenames — the diagrams never appeared when you opened the document. v2 embeds all 16 diagrams in this file. v1 gave each module a one-line purpose. v2 gives every module What it does / Why we need it / What happens if we skip it / Who uses it / Inputs → Outputs, plus example request/response JSON. And v1 mentioned MCP, RAG and multi-agent orchestration only as modules — v2 adds Part B, dedicated deep-dive chapters on Agentic AI, Multi-Agent Orchestration, MCP, RAG, LangGraph + Temporal, and LLM evals.

Contents
  1. How to use this book & conventions
  2. Chapter 0 — High-Level Design (numbered, 1–14)
  3. Part A — The 14 modules, M1–M14 (each: What / Why / Diagram / Components / APIs / Database / Sequence / Security / Gate)
  4. Part B — Agentic AI deep dives: B1 Agentic AI, B2 Multi-Agent Orchestration, B3 MCP, B4 RAG, B5 LangGraph + Temporal + Memory, B6 Evals & Observability
  5. Part C — Cross-cutting rules, user journeys, build order

1. How to use this book

Start at Chapter 0. Then build in order M2 → M3 → M4 → M5 → M6 → M7 → M1 → M8 → M9 → M10 → M11 → M12 → M13 → M14. Do not start a module until you have read its chapter and understood its gate. A module is done only when its gate passes. The cake rule (from SampAgent): at the end of every phase the app is fully working — build like layers of cake, not rings of onion.

Conventions (all modules): Spring Boot 3.x, Java 21, Spring Data JPA + Flyway, HikariCP, Postgres per service (schema = service name), JWT access 15 min / refresh 7 days with rotation, trace id on every request, PII redacted in logs, secrets in Azure Key Vault only, errors as {code, message, traceId}, pagination ?page&size&sort, idempotency key on all POST writes.

Chapter 0 — High-Level Design (numbered)

Numbers 1–14 are the chapters of Part A. Read top to bottom: Clients → Edge → Core services → AI → Data → Platform. A service talks to another service only over REST or Kafka — never by reading its database. The approval gate sits between the Coach Agent (M7) and any write. No agent approves its own work.

Figure 0 — EpitomeJob high-level design, modules numbered 1–14.

Part A — The 14 Modules

M1 — API Gateway

What it does: One front door for the whole system. Every request from Android, Web or the Recruiter Portal enters here first, and the Gateway decides: is this request authenticated, is it within its rate limit, and which service should handle it? It then forwards the request and returns the answer.
Why we need it: Without it, every service would have to check JWTs, rate limits and CORS itself — 14 copies of the same security code, 14 places to get it wrong. The Gateway is the one place where "who are you, and are you allowed in?" is answered.
If we skip it: Clients call services directly, security drifts apart per service, a flood of requests can take down the Matching Engine, and there is no single place to log or trace a request.

Who uses it: every client, every request. Inputs: HTTPS request + JWT. Outputs: routed response, or 401 / 429 / 503.

Internal components

ComponentResponsibility
RouteLocatorYAML routes per service, path /api/{service}/**. No business logic.
JwtFilterValidates JWT signature + expiry, extracts userId/roles, forwards X-User-Id, X-Roles, X-Trace-Id. Invalid → 401, no downstream call.
RateLimiterRedis token bucket: 100 req/min per user, 1000/min per service. Over → 429 + Retry-After.
CircuitBreakerResilience4j per route: opens after 5 failures in 10s, half-open probe, then 503 + fallback message.
AccessLoggerMethod, path, status, latency, trace id. Never bodies, never tokens.

APIs / CRUD

No business CRUD. Config only: GET /actuator/health, GET /actuator/routes (admin).

Database

None — stateless. Redis only: rate_limit:{userId} (counter, TTL 60s).

Sequence

  1. Client sends HTTPS + JWT.
  2. JwtFilter validates.
  3. RateLimiter checks.
  4. Route to target service.
  5. Log + return response.

How it connects to Agentic AI

The Coach Agent (M7) and MCP Server (M11) are reached only through the Gateway, so agent traffic gets the same auth, rate limiting and tracing as human traffic.

Gate: invalid JWT never reaches a service; 100 req/min enforced; a dead downstream service returns 503, not a hang.

M2 — Identity & Auth (Login)

What it does: Answers "who are you, and what may you do?" It registers users, checks passwords, issues JWT access + refresh tokens, handles Login with Google, forgot/reset password, roles (USER / COACH / ADMIN), and lockout after repeated failures. Every other service trusts its JWT — it never checks a password itself.
Why we need it: Without a single identity owner, each service would store its own users and passwords. That is how breaches happen. One owner, one password store, one token issuer — and every other module just verifies the token.
If we skip it: no login, no roles, no way to know whose resume or whose applications you are touching. The approval gate in M7 would have nobody to approve.

Who uses it: every user at login; every service on every request (token verification). Inputs: email + password, or a Google ID token. Outputs: access JWT (15 min) + refresh token (7 days, rotated).

Internal components

ComponentResponsibility / key methods
AuthControllerREST only, no business logic: POST /auth/register, /login, /refresh, /logout, /google, /forgot-password, /reset-password
AuthServiceOrchestrates register/login/refresh/logout; enforces lockout. register(dto), login(email, pw), refresh(token), logout(token)
JwtServiceRS256, Key Vault key. generateAccess(user), generateRefresh(user), verify(token), extractUserId(token)
PasswordServiceBCrypt cost 12. Never stores plain text. hash(pw), matches(pw, hash)
OAuth2Service (Google)Verifies Google ID token: checks aud = our client id, exp, email_verified. Links or creates the account. Never stores the Google token.
RoleServiceRBAC USER / COACH / ADMIN. hasRole(user, role), assignRole(admin, user, role)
LoginAttemptServiceCounts failures per email + IP; locks 15 min after 5 failures.
AuditServiceWrites login events to Kafka.

APIs / CRUD — with examples

POST /auth/login
{"email":"bala@example.com","password":"••••••••"}
→ 200 {"accessToken":"eyJ…","refreshToken":"…","expiresIn":900,
       "user":{"id":"…","email":"bala@example.com","role":"USER"}}

POST /auth/google
{"idToken":"google-id-token-from-the-app"}
→ verify with Google → link or create account → same 200 as above

POST /auth/refresh {"refreshToken":"…"} → 200 new pair (old token revoked)
POST /auth/logout  {"refreshToken":"…"} → 204 (that token revoked)

Register: validate email + password (≥8 chars, 1 upper, 1 digit) → BCrypt hash → insert user → verification email via M13 → 201. Duplicate email → 409. Wrong password → 401 with the generic message "Invalid credentials" (never say whether the email or the password was wrong). Refresh-token reuse (a revoked token presented again) → revoke all refresh tokens for that user (possible theft) + 401. Forgot password: always 200, never reveal whether the email exists.

Database — how it connects

Spring Data JPA, HikariCP (pool 10), Flyway migrations V1__identity.sql, schema identity, Postgres. The Repository is the only class that touches the DB — no raw SQL in Service or Controller.

TableColumnsIndexes
usersid UUID PK, email VARCHAR(255) UNIQUE NOT NULL, password_hash VARCHAR(60) NULL (NULL = Google-only), full_name VARCHAR(120), role VARCHAR(20) DEFAULT 'USER', status VARCHAR(20) DEFAULT 'ACTIVE', email_verified BOOLEAN, created_at, updated_at, last_login_atidx_users_email, idx_users_role
refresh_tokensid UUID PK, user_id UUID FK, token_hash VARCHAR(64) NOT NULL (SHA-256, never plain), expires_at, revoked BOOLEAN, created_atidx_refresh_user, idx_refresh_expires
oauth_accountsid UUID PK, user_id UUID FK, provider VARCHAR(20) ('GOOGLE'), provider_user_id VARCHAR(255), provider_email, UNIQUE(provider, provider_user_id)idx_oauth_provider_user
login_attemptsid UUID PK, email, ip VARCHAR(45), success BOOLEAN, attempted_atidx_attempts_email_time
rolesid UUID PK, name VARCHAR(20) UNIQUE — seeded USER, COACH, ADMIN—

Sequence — login

  1. Client → Gateway → AuthController.
  2. AuthService checks lockout → PasswordService.matches.
  3. JwtService generates access + refresh; refresh stored hashed.
  4. last_login_at updated; audit event to Kafka.
  5. 200 with tokens.

Google login: same, but OAuth2Service verifies the Google token first, then finds/links/creates the account.

How it connects to Agentic AI

The Coach Agent acts as the user: it carries the user's JWT when it calls tools, so a tool can never do more than that user could. The approval gate (M7) is tied to the user's identity — only that user can approve their own writes.

Security

BCrypt cost 12 · JWT RS256 + Key Vault · access 15 min · refresh rotation + reuse detection · lockout 5 failures / 15 min · generic 401 · no password in logs · HTTPS only · login rate-limited to 10/min per IP.

Gate: wrong password 5× locks the account; Google login creates/links correctly; reusing a revoked refresh token revokes all tokens for that user.

M3 — Profile Service

What it does: Holds the user's career profile — headline, summary, location, work type, salary range, skills, goals, preferences. It is the single source of truth for "who is this person professionally?"
Why we need it: Matching (M6), the Coach (M7) and Learning (M10) all need the same profile. Without one owner, each would keep its own copy and they would drift apart.
If we skip it: the agent matches jobs against a stale or missing profile, and the user has to re-enter their skills in three places.

Who uses it: the user, the Coach Agent, Matching, Learning. Inputs: profile fields. Outputs: profile + completeness score, profile.updated event.

Internal components

ProfileController (owner-only REST) · ProfileService (CRUD + completeness score) · SkillExtractor (normalises free-text skills to a controlled list) · PrivacyService (field visibility: public / coach-only / private; PII redaction) · ProfileValidator.

APIs / CRUD

POST /profiles · GET /profiles/me · PUT /profiles/me · GET /profiles/{id} (coach/admin, privacy-filtered) · POST /profiles/me/skills · DELETE /profiles/me/skills/{id} · POST /profiles/me/goals. Update is owner-only — the Service checks userId == token sub, not just the Controller. Delete is soft-delete (30 days, then hard delete) + event.

Database

JPA/Hikari/Flyway, schema profile. Tables: profiles (id, user_id UNIQUE, headline, summary, location, work_type, salary_min/max, currency, visibility, completeness, created/updated_at) · skills (id, profile_id FK, skill_name, level, years, UNIQUE(profile_id, skill_name)) · user_goals (id, profile_id FK, title, target_role, target_date, status) · preferences (id, profile_id FK UNIQUE, email_alerts, job_alerts, remote_only). Indexes: idx_profiles_user, idx_skills_name.

Sequence

  1. Client → Gateway → Controller.
  2. Service validates → PrivacyService filters.
  3. Repository saves → Kafka profile.updated.

How it connects to Agentic AI

The Coach reads the profile as long-term memory; Matching reads skills as the match input; Learning reads the target role as the gap-analysis target.

Gate: another user cannot read or write my profile; a profile update publishes an event that Matching consumes.

M4 — Resume Service

What it does: Stores resume files, parses them into text, extracts skills and experience, versions them (v1, v2 — old versions are kept, never overwritten), and embeds them for search. A resume is a file and the structured data inside it.
Why we need it: Everything downstream — matching, tailoring, interview prep — needs the resume as data, not as a PDF blob. Parsing it once, here, means every other module reads clean skills instead of re-parsing a PDF.
If we skip it: matching guesses from a profile the user typed by hand, tailoring has nothing to tailor, and every upload overwrites the last good resume.

Who uses it: the user (upload), Coach, Matching, RAG. Inputs: PDF/DOCX, max 10 MB. Outputs: resume metadata, parsed skills, embedding, resume.parsed event.

Internal components

ResumeController (multipart, PDF/DOCX only) · ResumeService (metadata, versioning) · PdfParser (Apache Tika, 30s timeout) · SkillExtractor · VersionService · EmbeddingClient (calls M12, async).

APIs / CRUD

POST /resumes  (multipart) → 202 {"resumeId":"…","status":"PARSING"}
  → async: parse → extract skills → embed → status "READY" → resume.parsed
GET /resumes/me · GET /resumes/{id} · DELETE /resumes/{id} (soft, blob deleted after 30 days)
POST /resumes/{id}/set-current/{version}

Errors: 400 bad type/size, 413 too large, 422 parse failed (file kept, status FAILED, user can re-upload).

Database

JPA/Hikari/Flyway, schema resume, Postgres for metadata; files in Blob (MinIO local / Azure Blob cloud), never in Postgres. Tables: resumes (id, user_id, blob_path, file_name, file_type, file_size, status, created_at) · resume_versions (id, resume_id FK, version, blob_path, is_current, UNIQUE(resume_id, version)) · resume_skills (id, resume_id FK, skill_name, years, confidence) · resume_embeddings (resume_id PK FK, embedding VECTOR(1536), model, updated_at — pgvector).

Sequence

  1. Upload → validate type/size → store blob → insert metadata + v1.
  2. Async parser → SkillExtractor → EmbeddingClient.
  3. Status READY → Kafka resume.parsed.

How it connects to Agentic AI

The Resume Agent (one of the 6 specialists) owns tailoring; it reads the parsed resume through MCP, never the raw PDF. RAG indexes the parsed text so the Coach can answer "what experience do I have in Spring Boot?" with a citation.

Gate: upload a real PDF → skills extracted → old version still retrievable after a v2 upload.

M5 — Job Discovery

What it does: Finds jobs and keeps them fresh. It ingests jobs from aggregators every 6 hours, normalises them (same fields, same format), deduplicates them (same title + company + location within 30 days = one job), indexes them for search, and fires alerts when a new job matches a saved search.
Why we need it: Without ingestion and dedup, the user sees the same job five times from five sources, and half the listings are expired. Discovery is a data pipeline, not a search box.
If we skip it: Matching has nothing to rank, alerts never fire, and the user goes back to searching job boards by hand.

Who uses it: Matching, Coach, the user (search). Inputs: aggregator feeds. Outputs: deduplicated jobs, search results, job.alert events.

Internal components

JobController (search API) · JobIngestService (scheduled, every 6h) · DedupService · SearchService (Postgres full-text in v1, Azure AI Search in cloud) · AlertService (saved searches → Kafka → M13).

APIs / CRUD

GET /jobs?q=&location=&workType=&page=&size= (cached in Redis 5 min) · GET /jobs/{id} · POST /jobs/saved-searches · DELETE /jobs/saved-searches/{id}. Ingest is internal only (scheduler, service token).

Database

JPA/Hikari/Flyway, schema jobs. Tables: jobs (id, external_id, source, title, company, location, work_type, salary_min/max, description, url, posted_at, expires_at, is_active, UNIQUE(source, external_id)) · job_sources (id, name UNIQUE, api_url, enabled, last_sync_at) · saved_searches (id, user_id, query JSONB) · job_alerts (id, user_id, saved_search_id FK, last_sent_at). Indexes: title, company, posted_at, full-text on title+description.

Sequence

  1. Scheduler → Ingest (aggregator API) → normalise → Dedup → insert/update → index.
  2. AlertService checks saved searches → Kafka → M13 sends the alert.
Gate: the same job from 2 sources appears once; ingest 100 jobs → deduplicated count is < 100 when duplicates exist.

M6 — Matching Engine

What it does: Ranks jobs for a resume and explains why each one matches. It does not just return a score — it returns the top 3 matching skills, the top 2 gaps, and the exact resume/JD lines that prove it, so the user can trust the ranking.
Why we need it: A ranked list without an explanation is a black box. Users ignore black boxes. The explanation is the product — it is what turns "here are 10 jobs" into "here is the job you should apply for, and here is what to fix first."
If we skip it: the user gets an unranked job list and has to read every description themselves. The Coach has no basis for recommending anything.

Who uses it: the user, the Coach Agent. Inputs: resume embedding + job embeddings. Outputs: ranked matches with explanations and citations.

Internal components

MatchController · EmbeddingService (resume embedding via M12, cached) · ScoringService (skills 50% + experience 30% + location/work-type 20% — weights in config, not code) · RankingService (top N, diversity: max 3 jobs from one company in the top 10) · ExplainService · FeedbackService (thumbs up/down, stored for re-weighting in v2).

APIs / CRUD

GET /matches?resumeId=…&limit=10
→ 200 [{"jobId":"…","score":87.5,"rank":1,
        "explanation":{"matchedSkills":["Spring Boot","Kafka"],
                       "gaps":["Azure APIM"],
                       "citations":["resume: line 12","jd: line 4"]}}]
POST /matches/{id}/feedback {"feedback":"UP"}
POST /matches/recompute {"resumeId":"…"}

Database

JPA/Hikari/Flyway, schema matching, Postgres + pgvector. Tables: matches (id, user_id, resume_id, job_id, score, rank, explanation JSONB, UNIQUE(user_id, resume_id, job_id)) · match_scores (id, match_id FK, skill_score, exp_score, location_score) · match_feedback (id, match_id FK, user_id, feedback 'UP'/'DOWN') · job_embeddings (job_id PK, embedding VECTOR(1536)).

Sequence

  1. Load resume embedding → pgvector nearest jobs → ScoringService → RankingService → ExplainService → store matches → response.
  2. Model unavailable → fallback to keyword score (never fail the whole request).

How it connects to Agentic AI

The Matching Agent is one of the 6 specialists. It does the ranking; the Supervisor decides what to do with the ranking (propose the top 3, ask the user, or tailor the resume for #1).

Gate: eval — 20 resume/JD pairs, the expected job is in the top 5 in ≥80%; every explanation cites real resume/JD lines, never invented skills.

M7 — Coach Agent (Supervisor)

What it does: The brain. The user says a goal in plain English — "Find me jobs and prepare me" — and the Coach plans it into steps, hands each step to the right specialist agent, checks the result, retries once if it fails, escalates to the user if it still fails, and proposes any write (apply, send, save) for the user to approve. It never executes a write itself.
Why we need it: One agent doing everything is fragile — it forgets steps, invents tools, and cannot be tested. A Supervisor that plans, delegates and checks is testable, recoverable (state in Postgres/Temporal, never in memory), and safe (the approval gate).
If we skip it: you have a chatbot, not an agent. It can talk about jobs, but it cannot do a multi-step job for you, and it cannot be trusted with anything that writes data.

Who uses it: the user (chat), all 6 specialists (as their caller). Inputs: a goal in plain English. Outputs: a plan, specialist results, and approval proposals.

Figure 7b — Multi-agent orchestration: Supervisor → 6 specialists → shared MCP + RAG → approval gate → data. See Part B, Chapter B2 for the full state machine.

Internal components

Supervisor (LangGraph graph: Plan → Route → Specialist → Check → Respond) · Planner (breaks a goal into steps with dependencies) · Router (picks the next specialist by step type) · MemoryService (short-term: current run; long-term: profile, goals, past plans — summarised, never raw chat history in the prompt) · ApprovalClient (creates a pending approval, pauses the Temporal workflow, resumes on Approve, cancels on Reject) · ToolClient (calls M11 MCP tools, never a service DB directly).

APIs / CRUD

POST /coach/chat {message} (SSE stream) · GET /coach/plans · GET /coach/plans/{id} · GET /coach/runs/{id} · Approvals: POST /approvals/{id}/approve | /reject.

Database

JPA/Hikari/Flyway, schema coach, Postgres. Tables: plans (id, user_id, goal TEXT, steps JSONB, status) · agent_runs (id, plan_id FK, user_id, status, started/finished_at) · agent_steps (id, run_id FK, step_no, specialist, input JSONB, output JSONB, status, error) · memories (id, user_id, summary TEXT, type) · approvals (id, user_id, run_id FK, action, payload JSONB, token_hash, status DEFAULT 'PENDING', expires_at 24h, decided_at). Approval token is signed (HMAC, Key Vault), idempotency key = approval id. Approve twice = one execution. Expired = 410.

Sequence — the graph

  1. Chat → Plan → Route → Specialist (via MCP tool) → Check.
  2. Check fails → retry once → still fails → escalate to the user (never guess).
  3. A write is needed → ApprovalClient creates an approval → graph PAUSES (Temporal).
  4. User Approves/Rejects → graph resumes/cancels → final answer (SSE).

Security

JWT + owner-only · tool calls authenticated service-to-service · prompt-injection guard (tool output is data, never an instruction) · PII redacted from LangSmith traces · agents never approve each other — only the human token holder can.

Gate: a write never executes without an approval; an expired approval never executes; a run survives a restart (state in Postgres/Temporal).

M8 — Interview Prep

What it does: Runs mock interviews for a specific job: picks 5 questions from the question bank (via RAG, matched to the role/company), asks them one by one (text or voice), scores each answer against a rubric (clarity, correctness, depth, communication — each 0–5), and returns a feedback report with 3 things to practise.
Why we need it: Practising alone does not tell you what to fix. A scored mock with a rubric does — and it reuses the same resume + JD the matching engine already knows.
If we skip it: the user walks into interviews unpractised, and the Coach cannot prepare them for a specific job.

Who uses it: the user, the Interview Agent. Inputs: jobId, answers (text/voice). Outputs: scores + feedback report.

Internal components

InterviewController · MockService (state machine: STARTED → QUESTION → ANSWER → SCORED → DONE) · VoiceService (STT via Whisper-compatible API, TTS for coach voice — audio in Blob, never in DB) · QuestionBank (RAG over M12) · RubricScorer (deterministic rubric, not free-text LLM score alone) · FeedbackService.

APIs / CRUD

POST /interviews/mock {jobId} → 201 with 5 questions · POST /interviews/{id}/answer {questionId, answerText | audio} → 200 with that answer's score · GET /interviews/{id}/feedback · GET /interviews/me.

Database

JPA/Hikari/Flyway, schema interview. Tables: interviews (id, user_id, job_id, status, started/finished_at) · interview_questions (id, interview_id FK, question_text, source, order_no) · interview_answers (id, question_id FK, answer_text, audio_path) · interview_scores (id, interview_id FK, clarity, correctness, depth, communication, overall, feedback). Audio deleted after 30 days unless the user saves it.

Gate: a mock runs end to end; the same answer scores the same twice; the feedback report contains 3 practises.

M9 — Application Tracker

What it does: Tracks every application on a kanban board (SAVED → APPLIED → INTERVIEW → OFFER → REJECTED), logs every status change, schedules follow-ups 7 days after applying, and drafts (never sends) recruiter follow-up messages.
Why we need it: Applications are the outcome the whole product exists for. Without a tracker, the user applies and forgets — no follow-up, no history, no idea which applications are stuck.
If we skip it: the Coach can find jobs and tailor resumes, but nothing records what was actually applied for.

Who uses it: the user, the Application Agent. Inputs: an approved proposal. Outputs: kanban board, follow-up reminders, drafts.

Internal components

TrackerController · TrackerService (kanban state machine — illegal transitions rejected, e.g. SAVED → OFFER) · FollowUpService (Temporal timer, 7 days) · OutreachDraftService (draft only) · DeadlineService.

APIs / CRUD

POST /tracker — only from an approved M7 proposal; a direct POST without an approval id is rejected 403 · GET /tracker?status= · PUT /tracker/{id}/status {toStatus} · POST /tracker/{id}/follow-up · GET /tracker/{id}. Every status change writes an application_events row.

Database

JPA/Hikari/Flyway, schema tracker. Tables: applications (id, user_id, job_id, resume_id, status DEFAULT 'SAVED', applied_at, UNIQUE(user_id, job_id)) · application_events (id, application_id FK, from_status, to_status, note) · follow_ups (id, application_id FK, due_at, status, sent_at) · outreach_drafts (id, application_id FK, draft_text, status DEFAULT 'DRAFT').

Gate: no application exists without an approval record; follow-up fires on schedule; status history is complete.

M10 — Learning Service

What it does: Closes skill gaps with a plan. It compares the user's resume skills against the skills target job descriptions ask for, reports the gap (missing + weak skills), builds a 30-60-90 roadmap (Weeks 1–4 foundations, 5–8 projects, 9–12 interview prep), serves courses and quizzes, and tracks weekly progress.
Why we need it: Matching tells you where you fall short; Learning tells you how to fix it. Without it, the gap report is a dead end.
If we skip it: the user knows they lack Azure APIM but has no plan, no courses, and no way to measure progress.

Who uses it: the user, the Learning Agent. Inputs: target role. Outputs: gap report, roadmap, quizzes, progress %.

Internal components

LearningController · GapAnalysisService (resume skills vs target JD skills) · RoadmapService · QuizService (questions from RAG, auto-graded) · ProgressService (weekly check-in).

APIs / CRUD

GET /learning/gap?targetRole= · POST /learning/roadmap {targetRole} · GET /learning/roadmap/{id} · POST /learning/quizzes/{id}/answer · PUT /learning/progress/{roadmapId} {pct}.

Database

JPA/Hikari/Flyway, schema learning. Tables: skill_gaps (id, user_id, target_role, skill_name, gap_level) · roadmaps (id, user_id, title, steps JSONB, status) · courses (id, title, provider, url, skill_name) · quizzes (id, course_id FK, question, answer) · progress (id, user_id, roadmap_id FK, week_no, pct_complete).

Gate: roadmap steps map 1:1 to the gaps found — no invented courses.

M11 — MCP Server

What it does: The universal plug for agents. It exposes every capability of EpitomeJob as a typed tool — search_jobs, parse_resume, update_profile, match_score, ask_docs — with a machine-readable schema, authentication, validation and audit. An agent never calls a service directly; it calls a tool here. See Part B, Chapter B3 for the full MCP deep dive.
Why we need it: Without MCP, every agent would need custom code for every service — and a new service would mean rewriting every agent. With MCP, a new tool is one annotated method, and every agent (ours, or a future external one) can discover and use it the same way.
If we skip it: agents call services ad hoc, with no schema, no audit, and no per-tool permission. One bad agent call can do anything, and nobody can prove what it did.

Who uses it: the Coach Agent and all 6 specialists. Inputs: JSON-RPC tools/call + arguments. Outputs: typed result, or a JSON-RPC error.

Internal components

McpController (STREAMABLE HTTP, /mcp, JSON-RPC) · ToolRegistry (discovers @McpTool methods at startup, publishes tools/list) · ResourceService (read-only resources: resume://{id}, job://{id}, profile://{id}) · PromptService (reusable prompts: tailor_resume, interview_prep) · ToolAuthFilter (JWT + per-tool role).

APIs

tools/list  → [{"name":"search_jobs","inputSchema":{…}}, …]
tools/call  {"name":"search_jobs","arguments":{"query":"Java Spring Boot"}}
            → validate args → auth → call M5 → audit → result
resources/list · resources/read · prompts/list · prompts/get

Database

JPA/Hikari/Flyway, schema mcp — tool registry + audit only, no business tables. Tables: mcp_tools (id, name UNIQUE, description, input_schema JSONB, service, enabled) · mcp_resources (id, uri UNIQUE, type) · mcp_prompts (id, name UNIQUE, template) · tool_calls_audit (id, tool_name, user_id, agent_run_id, args JSONB, result_status).

Security

JWT on every call · per-tool roles (apply_to_job requires an APPROVED context, search_jobs requires USER) · args validated (unknown field → -32602) · every call audited · tools cannot call each other in a loop (max depth 3).

Gate: an unauthenticated tools/call is rejected; every call appears in the audit table.

M12 — RAG Service

What it does: Answers questions from your documents, with citations — not from the model's memory. It ingests documents, chunks them (512 tokens, 50 overlap), embeds each chunk into a vector, stores the vectors in pgvector, and on a query runs hybrid search (lexical + vector), reranks the results, and returns the chunks with their source document and page/line. The Coach composes the answer from these chunks. See Part B, Chapter B4 for the full RAG deep dive.
Why we need it: A language model without RAG guesses — it invents skills, companies and dates. RAG is the difference between "the model said so" and "your resume, line 12, says so." It is also how the product stays honest when the model is small and local (Ollama).
If we skip it: every agent answer is a guess, matching explanations have no citations, and interview questions come from nowhere.

Who uses it: all agents and services. Inputs: a document, or a query. Outputs: ranked chunks + citations.

Internal components

RagController · IngestService · Chunker (512 tokens, 50 overlap, split on headings first) · EmbeddingService (Ollama nomic-embed-text local / Azure OpenAI in cloud) · HybridSearch (Postgres full-text + pgvector, merged) · Reranker (cross-encoder in v2, lexical score in v1) · CitationService.

APIs / CRUD

POST /rag/documents (upload) → 202, ingest async
GET  /rag/documents/me
POST /rag/query {"query":"…","topK":5}
→ 200 {"answer_context":[{"chunk":"…","source":"resume.pdf p2","score":0.91}],"citations":[…]}
DELETE /rag/documents/{id}  (chunks + embeddings deleted in the same transaction)

Database

JPA/Hikari/Flyway, schema rag, Postgres + CREATE EXTENSION vector. Tables: documents (id, user_id, title, blob_path, source_type) · chunks (id, document_id FK, chunk_no, content TEXT, page_no) · embeddings (chunk_id PK FK, embedding VECTOR(1536), model) · retrieval_logs (id, user_id, query, top_k, latency_ms). HNSW index: CREATE INDEX ON embeddings USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops).

Security

Tenant isolation — every query filters user_id = token sub. A query from User A never returns User B's chunks. PII redacted in retrieval logs.

Gate: eval — 50 questions, the correct document is cited in ≥90%; cross-user retrieval test passes.

M13 — Notification Service

What it does: Sends the right message, on the right channel, once. Email (SendGrid/SES), push (FCM), SMS (Twilio in v2) — from versioned templates only, never free-text from an agent. Every send is logged; a failed send retries 3 times with backoff, then goes to a dead-letter queue.
Why we need it: Approval requests, job alerts and follow-up reminders are useless if they never arrive — or if they arrive three times. One owner for delivery means one place for retries, opt-outs and logs.
If we skip it: the approval gate is silent (the user never knows something is waiting), alerts are lost, and a bug can spam a user 10 times.

Who uses it: Tracker, Coach, Billing (via Kafka events). Inputs: an event + template + payload. Outputs: a delivered message, or a dead-letter record.

Internal components

NotifyController (internal only) · EmailService · PushService · TemplateService (versioned templates: approval_request_v2, job_alert_v1) · DeliveryLogService · RetryService (exponential backoff, 3 attempts, then dead-letter).

APIs / CRUD

Internal: POST /notify/send {userId, channel, template, payload} (service token, not user JWT) · User: GET /notify/me · PUT /notify/me/channels (opt in/out per channel).

Database

JPA/Hikari/Flyway, schema notify. Tables: notifications (id, user_id, channel, template, payload JSONB, status DEFAULT 'QUEUED') · templates (id, name UNIQUE, version, subject, body, channel) · delivery_log (id, notification_id FK, provider, status, provider_id, attempted_at) · user_channels (id, user_id, channel, address, verified, UNIQUE(user_id, channel)).

Gate: a failed send retries 3× then dead-letters; a user who opted out receives nothing.

M14 — Billing & Analytics

What it does: Who pays, what they used, and whether the AI is getting better or worse. Plans (FREE / PRO / TEAMS), Stripe subscriptions, usage counting (LLM calls, tokens, storage) with limits, the LLM eval suite that runs on every deploy, and the append-only audit log every service writes to.
Why we need it: Two reasons. Money: without usage limits, one user can spend your whole Azure OpenAI budget. Quality: without an eval gate, a new prompt or model can silently make the AI worse — and you would ship it.
If we skip it: no revenue, no cost control, and no way to know the AI regressed until users complain.

Who uses it: the user (subscribe), admins (analytics), CI/CD (eval gate). Inputs: plan choice, Stripe webhooks, eval results. Outputs: subscription status, usage, eval scores, audit trail.

Internal components

BillingController · StripeService (checkout, webhooks, idempotent handling) · PlanService · UsageService (counts + enforces limits) · EvalService (LangSmith eval suite on every deploy) · AuditService (append-only).

APIs / CRUD

GET /billing/plans · POST /billing/subscribe {planId} → 200 {checkoutUrl} · POST /billing/webhook (Stripe signature verified, idempotent by stripe_event_id) · GET /billing/me · GET /admin/analytics (admin only).

Database

JPA/Hikari/Flyway, schema billing. Tables: plans (id, name UNIQUE, price_cents, llm_calls_limit, storage_mb) · subscriptions (id, user_id UNIQUE, plan_id FK, stripe_customer_id, stripe_subscription_id, status, current_period_end) · invoices (id, user_id, stripe_invoice_id UNIQUE, amount_cents, status) · usage (id, user_id, month, llm_calls, tokens, storage_mb, UNIQUE(user_id, month)) · audit_log (id, user_id, actor, action, resource, result — append-only, no UPDATE/DELETE) · evals (id, run_id, suite, score, passed).

Security

Stripe webhook signature verified (never trust an unsigned webhook) · no card data ever touches our DB · over limit → 402 + upgrade prompt.

Gate: the same webhook delivered twice creates one subscription; a deploy with a lower eval score is blocked.

Part B — Agentic AI Deep Dives

This is the part v1 was missing. MCP, RAG and multi-agent orchestration are not just three modules — they are the technologies that make EpitomeJob an agentic product instead of a CRUD app with a chatbot. Read these chapters before building M7, M11 or M12.

B1 — Agentic AI: what it is, and what it is not

What it is: an agent perceives a goal, plans steps, uses tools to act on real data, checks its own results, and asks a human before doing anything consequential. The loop is: Goal → Plan → Act (tool) → Observe → Check → (Approve) → Done. A chatbot stops at "talk". An agent finishes the job.

What it is not: a single LLM call with a clever prompt. That is a feature, not an agent. If it cannot call a tool, remember state across steps, retry on failure, or pause for approval, it is not agentic — and it should not be allowed near a write.

In EpitomeJob: the agent is the Coach (M7). Its tools are the MCP tools (M11). Its knowledge is RAG (M12). Its memory is Postgres + Temporal. Its safety is the approval gate. Remove any one of those and the agent is either useless or unsafe.

Agentic capabilityWhere it livesWhat happens without it
PlanningM7 Planner (LangGraph)Steps in the wrong order, or forgotten steps
ToolsM11 MCP ServerThe agent can talk but cannot act
KnowledgeM12 RAG ServiceHallucinated skills, jobs and dates
MemoryM7 MemoryService + PostgresEvery chat starts from zero
DurabilityTemporal (Part B5)A restart loses a half-finished job
Human-in-the-loopM7 ApprovalClientThe agent applies for jobs you never approved
EvaluationM14 EvalService + LangSmithSilent regressions ship to production

B2 — Multi-Agent Orchestration (Supervisor + 6 Specialists)

What it is: one Supervisor plans and checks; six specialists each do one job well. Specialists never talk to each other directly — they talk through the Supervisor, and they never approve each other's work.

SpecialistOne jobTools it uses (MCP)Reads from
Resume AgentParse + tailor a resume for a jobparse_resume, tailor_resumeM4, M12
Job Discovery AgentFind jobs for a profilesearch_jobsM5
Matching AgentRank + explain matchesmatch_scoreM6, M12
Interview AgentMock interview + scorestart_mock, score_answerM8, M12
Learning AgentGap analysis + roadmapgap_analysis, build_roadmapM10, M6
Application AgentDraft applications (never sends)draft_applicationM9

The LangGraph state machine: nodes Plan → Route → Specialist → Check → Respond. Edges are conditional on Check: pass → next step; fail → retry once → still fail → Escalate (ask the user, never guess). A write step goes Check → Propose → PAUSE (Temporal) → Approve/Reject → Resume/Cancel. State (plan, steps, results) is checkpointed to Postgres after every node, so a restart resumes mid-graph.

Patterns used: supervisor · sequential (resume before matching) · parallel (resume parse + job search at the same time) · handoff (clean context passed between specialists) · loop + retry once, then escalate · human-in-the-loop.

Example flow — "Find me jobs and prepare me": Plan (5 steps) → Resume Agent parses the resume → Job Discovery Agent searches → Matching Agent ranks top 5 with explanations → Interview Agent prepares a mock for #1 → Application Agent drafts the application → approval card → user Approves → Tracker records it. Total: 6 agents, 1 human decision.

B3 — MCP (Model Context Protocol) — deep dive

What it is: MCP is the standard plug between an AI agent and the tools it can use. Instead of the agent knowing how to call 14 services, it speaks one protocol — JSON-RPC over STREAMABLE HTTP at /mcp — and the MCP Server translates each tool call into a service call. Think USB for agents: any agent that speaks MCP can use any tool that speaks MCP.

Three primitives: Tools (things the agent can do: search_jobs, parse_resume, match_score — each with a JSON input schema, validated before execution) · Resources (things the agent can read: resume://{id}, job://{id} — read-only, no writes) · Prompts (reusable prompt templates: tailor_resume, interview_prep — versioned, so a prompt change is a deployment, not a guess).

Tool catalog (v1):

ToolCallsRequires
search_jobsM5USER
parse_resumeM4USER
match_scoreM6USER
ask_docsM12USER
update_profileM3USER + approval for writes
draft_applicationM9USER (draft only)
apply_to_jobM9APPROVED context only

Lifecycle of a tool call: Agent → tools/list (discovers the schema) → tools/call {name, arguments} → ToolAuthFilter (JWT + per-tool role) → schema validation (unknown field → -32602) → target service → result → audit row in tool_calls_audit → agent. Max tool-call depth 3 (no tool loops). Why MCP instead of direct REST from the agent: one protocol, one auth model, one audit trail, and a new tool is one @McpTool method — the agent discovers it automatically, no agent code changes.

B4 — RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) — deep dive

What it is: RAG is "open-book exam" for the model. Instead of answering from memory (closed-book — where hallucinations come from), the model first retrieves the relevant passages from your documents, then answers using only those passages, with a citation for each claim.

The pipeline: Ingest → Chunk (512 tokens, 50 overlap, split on headings first, so a chunk is one idea) → Embed (Ollama nomic-embed-text locally, Azure OpenAI in cloud — model name in config, never hardcoded) → Store (pgvector, HNSW index for fast nearest-neighbour search) → Query → Hybrid search (lexical Postgres full-text for exact terms like "Spring Boot" + vector for meaning like "Java backend framework" — merged, because each catches what the other misses) → Rerank (v1 lexical score, v2 cross-encoder) → Return top 5 chunks with source + page/line → Coach composes the answer from those chunks only.

Why hybrid, not just vector: vector search finds meaning but misses exact product names and numbers; lexical search finds exact terms but misses synonyms. A job that says "Spring Boot" and a resume that says "Java microservices" need both.

Rules: tenant isolation on every query (user_id = token sub) · delete a document and its chunks + embeddings are deleted in the same transaction · retrieval logs keep the query truncated to 200 chars (PII) · the RAG service never writes the final answer — it returns context, the Coach writes the answer, so the citation chain is auditable.

Eval: 50 fixed questions, the correct document must be cited in ≥90%. A prompt or embedding-model change that drops this score does not ship (M14 eval gate).

B5 — LangGraph + Temporal + Memory

LangGraph (Python 3.12+): the Supervisor is a graph, not a chain. Nodes are steps, edges are decisions, state is the plan + results so far. A chain cannot branch on a check result or loop back on a failure; a graph can. The graph runs in the Python LangGraph service; the Spring Boot backend is the system of record — Java owns the data, Python owns the reasoning. One contract between them, one source of truth.

Temporal: durable workflows. A multi-step job, a pending approval, and a scheduled follow-up are Temporal workflows — their state lives in Postgres/Temporal, so a restart mid-flight resumes instead of losing the job. Phase 4's recovery test (restart all containers mid-flight, verify state recovery) only works because of this. Never keep workflow state in memory.

Memory: short-term (current run: plan, steps, results — in the graph state) and long-term (profile, goals, past plans — summarised into memories, never raw chat history in the prompt, because raw history is slow, expensive and leaks PII into traces).

Approval gate, precisely: the graph proposes a write as an approvals row with the exact payload, a signed HMAC token and an idempotency key (= approval id). The graph pauses. The user approves or rejects in the app. Approve twice executes once. Expired (24h) executes never. This is what "human-in-the-loop" means in this system — a signed, expiring, idempotent proposal, not a chat message that says "ok".

B6 — LLM Evals, Observability & Cost

Evals: a fixed test set per AI module (Matching 20 resume/JD pairs, RAG 50 questions, Coach 10 goals). Every deploy runs the suite via LangSmith; the score is stored in M14 evals; a drop blocks the deploy. No eval gate, no AI deploy.

Observability: OpenTelemetry trace id on every request and every agent step, structured JSON logs, Grafana dashboards, alerts on p95 latency, error rate, approval backlog age, eval drop, and payment failures.

Cost: local Ollama is free (Dev/QA/PreProd run entirely on it). Production Azure OpenAI is not free — per-user token budgets, LLM call limits per plan (M14), and a cost dashboard. A prompt change that doubles tokens is a cost change, and it is reviewed as one.

Part C — Cross-cutting rules, journeys & build order

Errors (all modules)

{code, message, traceId} · 400 validation · 401 auth · 403 role/owner · 404 not found · 409 conflict · 410 expired approval · 429 rate-limited · 402 over limit (M14) · 500 generic (never a stack trace).

Events (Kafka)

profile.updated · resume.parsed · job.alert · approval.requested · approval.decided · application.status_changed · subscription.changed. Every event: {eventId, type, userId, payload, occurredAt}. Outbox pattern: write the event row in the same DB transaction as the business write, then publish.

User journeys (end to end)

Journey A — First job: Register (M2) → Profile (M3) → Upload resume (M4) → Search jobs (M5) → See 5 ranked jobs with explanations (M6) → Save one (M9, after approval) → Mock interview (M8).

Journey B — Coach does it: "Find me jobs and prepare me" → Coach plans (M7) → Resume, Job, Matching, Interview, Application specialists → approval card → Approve → application tracked (M9) → follow-up reminder (M13).

Journey C — Close a gap: Matching shows a gap (M6) → Learning builds a 30-60-90 roadmap (M10) → quizzes (M10) → progress tracked → re-match, score improves.

Build order

M2 Identity → M3 Profile → M4 Resume → M5 Job Discovery → M6 Matching → M7 Coach Agent (single-task first, then Supervisor) → M1 Gateway → M8 Interview → M9 Tracker → M10 Learning → M11 MCP → M12 RAG → M13 Notification → M14 Billing. Each module: read its chapter → build → run its gate → next module. Do not start M7 until M2–M6 gates pass.
